title: Idioms in Professional and Media English
learningObjectives: Recognize advanced idioms used in business and media contexts
Understand how idioms convey nuance in professional communication
Interpret idioms about decisions, challenges, and negotiations
Use advanced idioms appropriately in formal and semi-formal speech

sections.title: Idioms Beyond the Basics
sections.content: At an advanced level, idioms are everywhere — in news articles, business meetings, and everyday professional conversation. Knowing them well isn't just about vocabulary; it's about understanding tone and nuance. For example, when a journalist writes that a scandal left <the writing on the wall> for a company, native readers immediately understand the situation is doomed, without a single literal word about failure.

sections.title: Idioms in Business and Negotiation
sections.content:
Business English relies heavily on idiomatic expressions:

• <Get down to business> - Start focusing on important matters
• <Sit on the fence> - Avoid taking a clear position
• <Pull strings> - Use personal influence to get an advantage
• <A tough call> - A difficult decision
• <A ballpark figure> - An approximate estimate
• <Back to square one> - Starting over after a failed attempt

These phrases let speakers sound natural and precise at the same time.

sections.title: Idioms About Challenges and Resilience
sections.content:
When companies or people face difficulty, English has vivid idioms to describe it:

• <Weather the storm> - Survive a difficult period
• <A slippery slope> - A course of action likely to lead to worse outcomes
• <Fall through the cracks> - Be overlooked or forgotten
• <Wear many hats> - Perform many different roles
• <Under the radar> - Operating without being noticed

These idioms describe not just events, but attitudes toward adversity.

sections.title: A Story from the Business World
sections.content:
When the startup's biggest client canceled their contract, the founders knew it was time to <get down to business>. Some board members wanted to <sit on the fence> and wait, but the CEO refused. She had already seen <the writing on the wall> months earlier, so the team wasn't caught completely off guard. Still, rebuilding the client list meant going <back to square one>. Everyone had to <wear many hats>, and by the end of the year, the company had managed to <weather the storm>.

Can you find all five idioms in the story?

sections.title: Idioms About Making Decisions
sections.content:
Decision-making has its own set of idioms:

• <A game changer> - Something that significantly alters a situation
• <A level playing field> - A fair and equal situation for everyone
• <Read the room> - Understand the mood of the people present
• <Think on your feet> - Make quick decisions under pressure
• <Raise the bar> - Set a higher standard

Example: The new CEO's strategy was <a game changer> for the entire industry, forcing every competitor to <raise the bar>.

sections.title: Idioms in Mini Dialogues
sections.content:
Example 1: IN A MEETING - <A: Should we launch the product now or wait?
B: Let's not sit on the fence — I say we go for it.>

Example 2: AFTER A SETBACK - <A: The client backed out at the last minute.
B: Well, we'll just have to go back to square one.>

Example 3: GIVING FEEDBACK - <A: What did you think of her presentation?
B: Honestly, she really knows how to read the room.>

sections.title: Idioms and Register
sections.content:
Not every idiom fits every situation. In formal writing (reports, academic essays), idioms are often replaced with more neutral language:

• <Get to the bottom of> → investigate thoroughly
• <A step in the right direction> → a positive development
• <Think outside the box> → adopt an innovative approach

In spoken English and informal writing, however, idioms make speech sound natural and engaging. Advanced learners need to judge when an idiom is appropriate and when a more formal equivalent is expected.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.content:
Remember:

• Advanced idioms often appear in business, media, and professional speech
• Idioms can replace long explanations with a single vivid phrase
• Register matters — some idioms are too informal for academic writing
• Understanding idioms helps you catch nuance and tone, not just literal meaning
• Practice recognizing idioms in context rather than memorizing them in isolation

keyVocabulary.example: After the small talk, they got down to business.
Choosing who to promote was a tough call.
The company managed to weather the storm.

keyVocabulary.definition: Something that significantly alters a situation
keyVocabulary.example: The new app was a game changer for the industry.

keyVocabulary.definition: Understand the mood of the people present
keyVocabulary.example: A good speaker knows how to read the room.

keyVocabulary.definition: Starting over after a failed attempt
keyVocabulary.example: The deal fell through, so we're back to square one.

grammarPoints.explanation: Most idioms cannot be changed grammatically without losing their meaning — the words, tense, and structure stay fixed.
examples: The company weathered the storm. (not 'weathered a storm')
commonMistakes: Changing the preposition: 'on the fence' becomes meaningless as 'in the fence'
